paragraphs: Kolya leaned against the fence, trying to look dignified, and waited for Alyosha to appear. Yes, he had wanted to meet him for a long time. The boys had told him a great deal about Alyosha. Until now he had always put on a show of scornful indifference whenever Alyosha was mentioned, and he had even “criticized” what he heard. But secretly he longed to get to know him. Everything he was told about Alyosha was appealing and likable. So this moment mattered. To begin with, he had to show himself at his best and show his independence. “Or he’ll think I’m thirteen and take me for a boy, like the rest of them. And what are these boys to him? I’ll ask him once I know him better. It’s a pity I’m so short, though. Tuzikov is younger than I am, yet he’s half a head taller. But I have a clever face. I’m not good-looking. I know I’m hideous, but I’ve a clever face. I mustn’t talk too freely. If I throw myself into his arms all at once, he may think—Tfoo! How horrible if he should think—!”

These were the thoughts that stirred Kolya up while he did his utmost to look as independent as he could. What distressed him most was being so short. He did not mind his “hideous” face so much as his height. In a corner at home the year before, he had made a pencil mark on the wall to show how tall he was, and every two months since then he had anxiously measured himself against it to see how much he had gained. But alas, he grew very slowly, and this sometimes brought him almost to despair. His face was in fact by no means “hideous.” On the contrary, it was rather attractive, with fair, pale, freckled skin. His small, lively gray eyes had a fearless look and often glowed with feeling. He had rather high cheekbones and small, very red lips that were not very thick. His nose was small and unmistakably turned up. “I’ve a regular pug nose, a regular pug nose,” Kolya would mutter to himself when he looked in the mirror, and he always walked away from it indignant. “But perhaps I haven’t got a clever face?” he sometimes thought, doubting even that. But you must not suppose that his mind was taken up with his face and his height. On the contrary, however bitter the moments in front of the mirror were, he quickly forgot them, and forgot them for a long time, “abandoning himself entirely to ideas and to real life,” as he put it to himself.

Alyosha came out quickly and hurried over to Kolya. Before he reached him, Kolya could see that he looked delighted. “Can he really be so glad to see me?” Kolya wondered, feeling pleased. A word in passing: Alyosha’s appearance had changed completely since we last saw him. He had given up his cassock and now wore a well-cut coat and a soft round hat, and his hair was cropped short. All this suited him very well, and he looked quite handsome. His charming face always had a good-humored expression, but there was a gentleness and calm in his good humor. To Kolya’s surprise, Alyosha came out to him just as he was, without an overcoat. He had obviously come in a hurry. He held out his hand to Kolya at once.
“Here you are at last! We’ve been so eager to see you!”

“There were reasons, which you’ll hear in a moment. Anyway, I’m glad to meet you. I’ve been hoping for a chance for a long time, and I’ve heard a great deal about you,” Kolya muttered, a little breathless.
“We would have met anyway. I’ve heard a lot about you, too, but you’ve been a long time coming here.”
“Tell me, how are things going?”
“Ilusha is very ill. He’s certainly dying.”
“How awful! You have to admit that medicine is a fraud, Karamazov,” cried Kolya hotly.

“Ilusha has mentioned you often, very often, even in his sleep, in delirium, you know. You can see you used to be very, very dear to him ... before the incident ... with the knife.... Then there’s another reason.... Tell me, is that your dog?”
“Yes, Perezvon.”
“Not Zhutchka?” Alyosha looked at Kolya with eyes full of pity. “Is she lost forever?”

“I know you’d all like it to be Zhutchka. I’ve heard all about it.” Kolya smiled mysteriously. “Listen, Karamazov, I’ll tell you everything. That’s what I came for. That’s why I asked you to come out here, to explain the whole episode to you before we go in,” he began with animation. “You see, Karamazov, Ilusha came into the preparatory class last spring. Well, you know what our preparatory class is—a crowd of small boys. They started teasing Ilusha right away. I’m two classes higher up, and of course I only watched them from a distance. I saw the boy was small and weak, but he wouldn’t give in to them. He fought them. I saw he was proud, and his eyes were full of fire. I like children like that. And they teased him all the more. The worst of it was that he was dressed horribly at the time. His breeches were too small for him, and there were holes in his boots. They hounded him about it and jeered at him. That I can’t stand. I stood up for him at once and gave it to them hot. I beat them up, but they adore me, you know, Karamazov?” Kolya boasted impulsively. “But I’m always fond of children. I’ve got two chicks in my hands at home right now—that’s what held me up today. So they stopped beating Ilusha, and I took him under my protection. I saw the boy was proud. I tell you, the boy was proud. But in the end he became slavishly devoted to me. He did my slightest bidding, obeyed me as if I were God, tried to copy me. Between classes he’d run straight to me, and I’d walk around with him. On Sundays, too. They always laugh when an older boy makes friends with a younger one like that, but that’s a prejudice. If it’s my fancy, that’s enough. I’m teaching him, developing him. Why shouldn’t I develop him if I like him? Here you are, Karamazov, taking up with all these nestlings. I see you want to influence the younger generation—to develop them, to be of use to them. And I assure you, this trait in your character, which I knew by hearsay, attracted me more than anything. Let’s get to the point, though. I noticed that a sort of softness and sentimentality was coming over the boy, and you know, I positively hate this sheepish sentimentality. I’ve hated it since I was a baby. There were contradictions in him, too. He was proud, but he was slavishly devoted to me, and yet all at once his eyes would flash and he’d refuse to agree with me. He’d argue, fly into a rage. Sometimes I’d put forward certain ideas, and I could see it wasn’t so much that he disagreed with the ideas. He was simply rebelling against me, because I was cool in answering his affection. And so, to train him properly, the tenderer he was, the colder I became. I did it on purpose. That was my idea. My aim was to form his character, to knock him into shape, to make a man of him ... and besides ... no doubt you understand me at a word. Then suddenly I noticed that for three days in a row he was downcast and dejected, not because of my coldness, but for something else, something more important. I wondered what the tragedy was. I pumped him and found out that he had somehow got to know Smerdyakov, who was footman to your late father—this was before his death, of course—and Smerdyakov had taught the little fool a silly trick—that is, a brutal, nasty trick. He told him to take a piece of bread, stick a pin in it, and throw it to one of those hungry dogs that snap up anything without chewing, and then to watch and see what would happen. So they prepared a piece of bread like that and threw it to Zhutchka, that shaggy dog there’s been such a fuss about. The people of the house it belonged to never fed it at all, though it barked all day. (Do you like that stupid barking, Karamazov? I can’t stand it.) So it rushed at the bread, swallowed it, and began to squeal. It spun round and round and ran away, squealing as it went out of sight. That was Ilusha’s own account of it. He confessed it to me and cried bitterly. He hugged me, shaking all over. He kept repeating, ‘He ran away squealing.’ The sight of it haunted him. He was tormented by remorse, I could see that. I took it seriously. I decided to teach him a lesson for other things as well. So I have to admit I wasn’t quite straightforward, and I pretended to be more indignant than I perhaps was. ‘You’ve done a nasty thing,’ I said, ‘you’re a scoundrel. I won’t tell on you, of course, but I’m going to have nothing to do with you for a while. I’ll think it over and let you know through Smurov’—that’s the boy who just came with me, he’s always ready to do anything for me—‘whether I’ll have anything to do with you in the future or whether I give you up for good as a scoundrel.’ He was tremendously upset. I have to own I felt I’d gone too far as I spoke, but there was no help for it. I did what I thought best at the time. A day or two later I sent Smurov to tell him that I would not speak to him again. That’s what we call it when two schoolfellows refuse to have anything more to do with each other. Secretly I only meant to send him to Coventry for a few days and then, if I saw signs of repentance, to hold out my hand to him again. That was my intention. But what do you think happened? He heard Smurov’s message, and his eyes flashed. ‘Tell Krassotkin from me,’ he cried, ‘that I’ll throw bread with pins to all the dogs—all—all of them!’ ‘So he’s going in for a bit of temper. We’ll have to smoke it out of him.’ And I began to treat him with contempt. Whenever I met him I turned away or smiled sarcastically. And just then that affair with his father happened. You remember? You have to realize he was already fearfully worked up by what had happened. The boys, seeing I’d given him up, set on him and taunted him, shouting, ‘Wisp of tow, wisp of tow!’ Soon he was having regular skirmishes with them, which I’m very sorry about. They seem to have given him one very bad beating. One day he flew at them all as they were coming out of school. I stood a few yards off, looking on. And I swear, I don’t remember laughing. It was quite the other way. I felt awfully sorry for him, and in another minute I’d have run up to take his side. But he suddenly met my eyes. I don’t know what he imagined, but he pulled out a penknife, rushed at me, and stabbed at my thigh, here in my right leg. I didn’t move. I don’t mind owning I can be plucky sometimes, Karamazov. I simply looked at him with contempt, as if to say, ‘This is how you repay all my kindness! Do it again, if you like, I’m at your service.’ But he didn’t stab me again. He broke down, he was frightened at what he’d done, he threw away the knife, burst out crying, and ran off. I didn’t sneak on him, of course, and I made them all keep quiet so it wouldn’t reach the ears of the masters. I didn’t even tell my mother till it had healed. And the wound was a mere scratch. And then I heard that the same day he’d been throwing stones and had bitten your finger—but you understand now what a state he was in! Well, it can’t be helped. It was stupid of me not to come and forgive him—that is, to make it up with him—when he was taken ill. I’m sorry for it now. But I had a special reason. So now I’ve told you all about it ... but I’m afraid it was stupid of me.”

“Oh, what a pity,” exclaimed Alyosha with feeling, “that I didn’t know before what terms you were on with him! I’d have come to you long ago to beg you to go to him with me. Would you believe it, when he was feverish he talked about you in delirium. I didn’t know how much you meant to him! And you really haven’t managed to find that dog? His father and the boys have been hunting all over the town for it. Would you believe it, since he’s been ill I’ve heard him three times say, in tears, ‘It’s because I killed Zhutchka, father, that I’m ill now. God is punishing me for it.’ He can’t get that idea out of his head. And if the dog were found and proved to be alive, one might almost imagine the joy would cure him. We’ve all rested our hopes on you.”
“Tell me, what made you hope I’d be the one to find him?” Kolya asked, with great curiosity. “Why did you count on me rather than anyone else?”

“There was a report that you were looking for the dog, and that you’d bring it when you’d found it. Smurov said something like that. We’ve all been trying to persuade Ilusha that the dog is alive, that it’s been seen. The boys brought him a live hare. He just looked at it with a faint smile and asked them to set it free in the fields. And so we did. His father has just this moment come back, bringing him a mastiff pup, hoping to comfort him with that. But I think it only makes things worse.”
“Tell me, Karamazov, what sort of man is the father? I know him, but what do you make of him—a mountebank, a buffoon?”

“Oh, no. There are people of deep feeling who have somehow been crushed. Buffoonery in them is a form of bitter irony against those to whom they don’t dare speak the truth, because for years they’ve been humiliated and intimidated by them. Believe me, Krassotkin, that sort of buffoonery is sometimes tragic in the extreme. His whole life now is centered on Ilusha, and if Ilusha dies, he will either go mad with grief or kill himself. I’m almost certain of that when I look at him now.”
“I understand you, Karamazov. I see you understand human nature,” Kolya added, with feeling.
“And as soon as I saw you with a dog, I thought it was Zhutchka you were bringing.”

“Wait a bit, Karamazov, maybe we’ll find it yet. But this is Perezvon. I’ll let him go in now, and perhaps it will amuse Ilusha more than the mastiff pup. Wait a bit, Karamazov, you’ll know something in a minute. But I say, I’m keeping you here!” Kolya cried suddenly. “You’ve no overcoat on in this bitter cold. You see what an egoist I am. Oh, we’re all egoists, Karamazov!”
“Don’t worry. It is cold, but I don’t often catch cold. Let’s go in, though. And by the way, what’s your name? I know you’re called Kolya, but what else?”
“Nikolay—Nikolay Ivanovitch Krassotkin, or, as they say in official documents, ‘Krassotkin son.’” Kolya laughed for some reason, but then added suddenly, “Of course I hate my name Nikolay.”
“Why is that?”
“It’s so trivial, so ordinary.”
“You’re thirteen?” asked Alyosha.

“No, fourteen—that is, I’ll be fourteen very soon, in two weeks. I’ll confess one weakness of mine, Karamazov, just to you, since it’s our first meeting, so you can understand my character right away. I hate being asked my age. More than that ... and in fact ... there’s a libelous story going around about me, that last week I played robbers with the preparatory boys. It’s a fact that I did play with them, but it’s a perfect libel to say I did it for my own amusement. I have reasons to believe you’ve heard the story. But I wasn’t playing for my own amusement. It was for the sake of the children, because they couldn’t think of anything to do by themselves. But they’ve always got some silly tale. This is an awful town for gossip, I can tell you.”
“But what if you had been playing for your own amusement? What’s the harm?”
“Come now, for my own amusement! You don’t play horses, do you?”

“But you have to look at it this way,” said Alyosha, smiling. “Grown-up people go to the theater, and there the adventures of all sorts of heroes are acted out—sometimes there are robbers and battles, too. Isn’t that just the same thing, in a different form, of course? And young people’s games of soldiers or robbers at playtime are also art in its first stage. You know, they spring from the growing artistic instincts of the young. And sometimes these games are much better than performances in the theater. The only difference is that people go there to look at the actors, while in these games the young people are the actors themselves. But that’s only natural.”

“You think so? Is that your idea?” Kolya looked at him intently. “Oh, you know, that’s rather an interesting view. When I get home, I’ll think it over. I’ll admit I thought I might learn something from you. I’ve come to learn from you, Karamazov,” Kolya concluded, in a voice full of spontaneous feeling.
“And I from you,” said Alyosha, smiling and pressing his hand.
Kolya was very pleased with Alyosha. What struck him most was that Alyosha treated him exactly as an equal and talked to him just as if he were “quite grown up.”
“I’ll show you something in a moment, Karamazov. It’s a theatrical performance, too,” he said, laughing nervously. “That’s why I’ve come.”
“Let’s go first to the people of the house, on the left. All the boys leave their coats in there, because the room is small and hot.”

“Oh, I’m only coming in for a minute. I’ll keep my overcoat on. Perezvon will stay here in the passage and be dead. _Ici_, Perezvon, lie down and be dead! You see how he’s dead. I’ll go in first and scout around, then I’ll whistle to him when I think the time is right, and you’ll see, he’ll dash in like mad. Only Smurov mustn’t forget to open the door at the right moment. I’ll arrange it all, and you’ll see something.”
